catalog_quote: In Thangmi, stress is non-distinctive, prosodic and relatively unpronounced. In glossary entries in the lexicon, stress is indicated by a stress mark [ "] before the stressed syllable, but only in instances when it is not predictable. Unless otherwise indicated, all Thangmi words are stressed on the first syllable. The only deviations from this rule relate to Thangmi verb forms composed of three syllables of more, in which the stress falls on the second syllable: ... hara what? [two syllables] ["hara] ... akyarak the bulb of an arum lily, Arum campanulatum ["akjarak}] [three syllables] ... bosa to grow (of crops) [two syllables] ["boßa] ... kerepsa to cry, weep [three syllables] [kE"rEpßa] ... cinampasa to cause to amuse, make play [four syllables] [tsi"nampaßa] ... Reflexive verbs follow a slightly different pattern with regard to word and syllable stress. Since the reflexive marker <-si> (REF) is never stressed, the stress always falls on the preceding syllable, as in the examples below: ... phaksisa to eat by throwing a mouthful at a time into the ["pÓakßißa] mouth [three syllables] ... thaffarafsisa to lie on one's back without sleeping [thaNNa"raNßißa] [five syllables] ... Inflected verb forms do not deviate from the above rules, as shown in the examples below: ... kerep-fa-n I cried [three syllables] [kE"rEpNan] ... thaffaraf-si-fa-du I am lying on my back without sleeping [thaNNa"raNßiNad1u] [six syllables]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is not contrastive and is weakly realised. Default: first syllable of the word (nouns, adjectives, one- and two-syllable verbs, e.g. ['hara] 'what?', ['akjarak] 'arum bulb', ['bosa] 'to grow'). Exception: verb forms (stems and inflected forms) of three or more syllables carry stress on the second syllable (e.g. [kE'rEpsa] 'to cry', [tsi'nampasa] 'to cause to play', [kE'rEpNan] 'I cried'). The reflexive suffix -si is never stressed, so in reflexive verbs stress stays on the syllable preceding -si (e.g. ['phaksisa], [thaNNa'raNsisa]). Unpredictable cases are marked in the lexicon.
new_statements.exceptions: Verb forms of three or more syllables (second-syllable stress); reflexive verbs (stress on the syllable before -si); lexical entries with unpredictable stress are marked with a stress mark in the glossary; Nepali loans may deviate from the canonical syllable scheme (fn. 7).
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (citation forms and inflected verb forms); a separate phrase/sentence-level prosodic accent is realised as vowel lengthening (section 5, p. 101). The article describes the Dolakha dialect of Thangmi.
new_statements.identity_note: Turin 2004 explicitly describes the phonology of the Dolakha dialect of Thangmi (Glottolog than1259 covers the language as a whole; Turin notes two mutually unintelligible dialects, Dolakha and Sindhupalcok). The name Thami (Nepali) is the same language.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and weak; every word is stressed on the first syllable, except verb forms of three or more syllables, which are stressed on the second syllable (kerepsa 'to cry' [kɛˈrɛpsa], cinampasa [tsiˈnampasa]); the reflexive suffix -si is never stressed, so in reflexive verbs stress falls on the syllable before it (phaksisa [ˈphaksisa], thangngarangsisa [thaŋŋaˈraŋsisa]); inflected forms follow the same rules (boy-an [ˈbojan], kerep-nga-n [kɛˈrɛpŋan]). Note the text layer renders the IPA stress mark as a double quote ["] because of a legacy font.
new_statements.exceptions: Verb forms of three or more syllables take second-syllable stress; the reflexive marker -si is never stressed, so stress precedes it; lexicon entries mark stress only where it is unpredictable. Section 4 (p. 180) adds that vowels lengthen 'for emphasis or as the result of bearing the prosodic accent of a clause or sentence', chiefly in adjectives, adverbs and interjections (phrase-level, not word stress).
new_statements.identity_note: The dissertation focuses on the Dolakhâ dialect of Thangmi (preface, p. xxv-xxvi: 'Although I eventually opted to focus on the Dolakhâ dialect.. examples of both spoken forms feature in this monograph'); the Sindhupâlcok dialect is treated comparatively in Chapter 2 and its differences from Dolakhâ concern segments (glottalisation of -k, sibilants, vowel opening), not stress. The stress rule is stated for Thangmi generally with no dialect qualification.
